*   **Photometric Variation:** Standard metrics like PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS are difficult to interpret on datasets with significant photometric variation because they penalize global brightness/color shifts [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that 'The metrics used elsewhere in this paper (PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS) are difficult to draw meaningful conclusions from due to the aforementioned photometric variation.' It further explains that models attempting to explain away photometric variation perform poorly on these metrics because they modify brightness/color, whereas the proposed method neutralizes this variation. This directly supports the claim that these metrics are difficult to interpret on datasets with significant photometric variation because they penalize global brightness/color shifts.

5.  **Test-Time Inference:** To generate a consistent reconstruction, set the embedding vector to zero ($e_i = \mathbf{0}$) for all rays [S1].

The claim states that to generate a consistent reconstruction, the embedding vector is set to zero for all rays at test-time. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in the passages: 'When we evaluate this model variant at test-time, we set the embedding vector to 0. This gives us a pleasing looking reconstruction... and that is consistent across all images'. The bullet points in the source notes also state: 'At test-time, set the embedding vector to 0 to produce a reconstruction corresponding to the photometric average of all input cameras.' Thus, the evidence fully supports the claim.

This method extends the standard NeRF MLP architecture by learning a distinct per-image embedding vector for each scene, which is injected into the color prediction network to account for view-dependent photometric variations [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the model variant 'learns a per-image embedding for each scene and uses that embedding within the NeRF MLP when predicting color.' It further explains that this approach is used to handle photometric variation, contrasting it with methods that modify scene brightness/color to explain camera variation. The claim accurately reflects these details found in the source text.
supported

It sets itself apart from standard NeRF by explicitly modeling global appearance shifts across input views, and differs from [SVS](link) by neutralizing this variation during training to yield consistent global brightness and color across views [S1].

The claim states that the model differs from standard NeRF by modeling global appearance shifts (via per-image embeddings) and differs from SVS by neutralizing this variation during training to yield consistent brightness/color. The evidence explicitly supports both parts: 1) It mentions a variant that 'learns a per-image embedding... and injects it into the NeRF MLP' (modeling appearance shifts). 2) It explicitly states 'Unlike SVS which modifies scene brightness/color to explain camera variation, GLO neutralizes photometric variation during training, yielding consistent global brightness/color across views.' This matches the claim's description of the difference from SVS.
supported
The sources note that the "w/GLO" model performs poorly on these raw metrics compared to baselines that attempt to "explain away" variation, but produces visually consistent results [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the 'w/GLO' model variant 'performs quite poorly' on standard metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) because it learns per-image embeddings. It contrasts this with baselines like SVS which 'attempt to explain away photometric variation' by modifying brightness/color. Furthermore, the evidence notes that the 'w/GLO' model produces a 'pleasing looking reconstruction' that is 'consistent across all images' (visually consistent results). Thus, every part of the claim is directly supported by the text.
supported

Use when the input dataset exhibits significant per-image photometric variation (e.g., lighting changes, exposure differences) and the goal is to produce a consistent, canonical view synthesis rather than reproducing the exact lighting of each source image [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the model variant (specifically the 'w/GLO' variant) learns a per-image embedding and that setting this embedding to zero at test-time produces a reconstruction corresponding to the 'photometric average' which is 'consistent across all images'. It further contrasts this with SVS, which attempts to 'explain away' photometric variation. The text identifies 'photometric variation' (lighting/exposure differences) as a key challenge and positions the proposed method's ability to neutralize this variation to create a consistent view as a primary goal and feature.
